passage:
Tuesday night.
Today at lunch my best friend Payal called me "Professor Glasses" again. Usually I laugh, because she only says it when I win the quiz, and I call her "Speedy Noodle" because she finishes her tiffin in two minutes. We both crack up.
But this morning the eye doctor told Mummy I need thicker lenses, and a few boys were already sniggering at my new frames. Payal said it loudly and pushed my specs up my nose.
I didn't laugh. I just looked at my dal.
She kept grinning for a second, then stopped. "Hey. Too much?"
I nodded.
She said sorry and never said it again all afternoon. On the bus she gave me half her mango slice.
Maybe tomorrow it will feel funny again. Not yet.
- Manoj

qa.q: What nickname did Payal call Manoj at lunch?
qa.a: She called Manoj "Professor Glasses" again.

qa.q: What was Manoj most likely feeling when the nickname came up today, and what else could the silence mean?
qa.a: Manoj most likely felt hurt and embarrassed, because the joke came on the same day as the thicker lenses and the boys' sniggering. The silence could also have been plain tiredness, which is why asking was better than guessing.

qa.q: Which choice of Payal's worked, and why?
qa.a: Stopping mid-grin to ask "Too much?" worked, because it gave Manoj a chance to say yes and the teasing ended before it hurt more.

qa.q: How might Payal have seen the joke differently from Manoj today?
qa.a: To Payal it was the same friendly nickname as always, tied to quiz wins; she probably did not know the new lenses had turned it into a sore spot until Manoj went quiet.

grounding: The diary shows a shared nickname that is usually affectionate becoming hurtful when it touches a fresh sore spot, and the friend checking in once the narrator goes quiet.

On the dusty ground behind the panchayat office, the boys played cricket until the sun turned orange. Madhav bowled; Sahil swung and missed.
"Arre Sahil, you bat like a buffalo chasing a fly!" Madhav shouted. Sahil laughed and swished the bat behind him like a tail.
Then Madhav flapped his arms and fell sideways into the dust, copying how Sahil had tumbled off his cycle at the temple fair while half the village watched. The other boys hooted.
Sahil's grin went flat. He picked at the tape on the bat handle and said nothing.
Madhav began a second fall, saw Sahil's face, and stopped halfway. He dusted his knees and walked over. "The fair thing still bad?"
Sahil shrugged, then nodded once.
"Okay. Buffalo only, no cycle," Madhav said, and Sahil gave a small smile.

qa.q: What did Madhav copy that made the other boys hoot?
qa.a: Madhav copied how Sahil had tumbled off his cycle at the temple fair.

qa.q: How can you tell Sahil felt differently about the two jokes?
qa.a: Sahil laughed and played along with the buffalo joke, but after the cycle fall his grin went flat and he picked at the tape in silence, which suggests he felt embarrassed and hurt. He might also have been tired, which is why Madhav asked.

qa.q: What small step helped turn things around?
qa.a: Madhav stopped halfway through the second fall and asked a short, direct question, then dropped the sore joke and kept the one Sahil enjoyed.

qa.q: If you were one of the boys who hooted, what might you notice next time?
qa.a: You might notice that Sahil laughed at one joke and went silent at the other, and that hooting along can keep a painful memory going.

grounding: The village cricket scene contrasts a safe shared joke with one that hits a sore memory, and shows the teaser stopping to check when the friend goes quiet.

Rosa and Freya walked home through the park in Leeds, kicking wet leaves.
"Your hat looks like a tea cosy," Rosa said, and Freya laughed so hard she snorted.
"Your wellies look like two frogs," Freya shot back. They were both giggling.
Then Rosa sang, "Tea Cosy Girl, do the solo you messed up!"
Freya's laugh stopped. She tugged the hat lower and walked faster, eyes on the path.
Rosa hurried to catch up. "Hey. Was that a bad one? I'll stop."
Freya was quiet for a few steps. "The solo thing, yeah. Mrs Hale sighed at me in front of the whole choir."
"Sorry. That's off the list," Rosa said.
Freya bumped her shoulder. "The tea cosy can stay, though." 🙂

qa.q: What did Freya say Rosa's wellies looked like?
qa.a: Two frogs.

qa.q: What was Freya feeling when Rosa mentioned the solo, and what is one other reading of her walking faster?
qa.a: Freya most likely felt embarrassed and stung, since Mrs Hale had sighed at her in front of the choir. Walking faster could also have meant she was simply cold or wanted to get home, so Rosa's question was the way to find out.

qa.q: What went right after the joke landed badly?
qa.a: Rosa noticed the change, caught up, asked instead of guessing, and promised to drop the solo joke, while the safe hat joke stayed as a shared laugh.

qa.q: How might the walk have ended if Rosa had kept singing?
qa.a: Freya would probably have felt mocked about a real embarrassment, and a fun walk could have turned into a hurtful one.

grounding: Two friends trade safe, affectionate insults until one joke touches a sore spot, and the teaser checks in when her friend goes quiet.

passage:
The birthday party on the fourth floor was loud with older girls from Sharmila's class, and Rukmini stood near the balloons holding a paper cup she had not drunk from.
When the cake was finished, someone said, "Anyone know a good joke?"
Rukmini's cheeks went warm. "Why couldn't the bicycle stand up on its own?"
Nobody knew.
"Because it was two-tired!"
For a second, silence. Then Sharmila groaned, "Nooo, that's terrible," and flopped on the sofa laughing. Two girls repeated it to each other: "Two-tired, too tired!"
"I have one about a cheese too," Rukmini said, a little louder.
"Go on then," Sharmila said, moving her feet so Rukmini could sit.
By the time the auto came, Rukmini had told six riddles and was sitting in the middle of the sofa.

qa.q: How many riddles had Rukmini told by the time the auto came?
qa.a: Rukmini had told six riddles.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini tell the bicycle riddle, and how do her cheeks and cup hint at her mood?
qa.a: She probably wanted to join the older girls: the untouched cup and warm cheeks suggest she felt shy and nervous at first, and sharing a joke was a way in. She may also simply have loved that riddle and wanted someone to hear it.

qa.q: What made the riddle work as a way into the group?
qa.a: It was short, depended on a double meaning everyone could catch, and gave the others something to repeat and groan at together.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have seen Rukmini before and after the joke?
qa.a: Before, Rukmini was probably just a quiet guest by the balloons; after the pun, Sharmila treated her as part of the fun and made room on the sofa.

grounding: The party shows a school-age child using a pun based on a double meaning to share fun and become part of a group.

"Didi, Didi, what has hands but can't clap?"
Usha didn't look up from her maths. "A clock. You asked me yesterday."
"Okay, okay, new one. I made it myself." Arnab climbed onto the bed. "Why is the ceiling fan a good friend?"
"Arnab, I have twelve sums."

Usha put her pencil down. "That's... actually not bad."
"Really?"
"Who taught you that?"
"Nobody. I was lying under it and thinking." Arnab grinned. "Tomorrow I'll tell it in class."
"Tell it after the prayer, when Sir is in a good mood."
"Will you be my fan?"

qa.q: How can you tell Arnab felt proud of his joke?
qa.a: He announced he made it himself, spread his arms for the punchline, explained both meanings of "fan", and asked "Really?" when Usha praised it, which shows he felt proud and eager for her approval. 😊

qa.q: What advice did Usha give, and why might it help?
qa.a: She suggested telling it after prayer when the teacher is in a good mood, which helps Arnab share his fun at a moment the group is ready to enjoy it.

My first week at the hostel in the hills, I didn't know anybody. I ate fast and went back to my bunk.
On the fourth evening, Dolma leaned over from the next bed. "Knock knock."
I stared at her. "Who's there?"
"Lettuce."
"Lettuce who?"
"Lettuce in, it's freezing out here!"
Half the dorm laughed. I didn't, because I was too busy thinking about how one word could be two words at once.
The next night I was ready. "Knock knock," I said to Dolma. My voice shook a little.
"Who's there?"
"Tank."
"Tank who?"
"You're welcome!"
Dolma laughed so loudly the warden knocked on the door. After that, the whole row of bunks swapped jokes before lights out, and I was in the middle of it.
- Pranav

qa.q: What word did Dolma use in her knock-knock joke?
qa.a: Lettuce.

qa.q: What might Pranav have been feeling when saying the first knock-knock joke?
qa.a: Pranav was probably nervous, since the voice shook, but also hopeful of joining in; staying quiet at Dolma's joke may have been curiosity about the wordplay rather than not finding it funny.

qa.q: What would you advise a new child who feels left out in a hostel?
qa.a: Try sharing something small and fun, like a joke or riddle, with one friendly person first; it can open the door to the whole group.

qa.q: How might Dolma have seen Pranav's first joke?
qa.a: Dolma likely felt pleased that the quiet newcomer had answered her game with a joke of their own, and her loud laugh welcomed Pranav in.

grounding: Looking back, the narrator shows wordplay jokes as both a sign of noticing double meanings and a way to join a group.

In Class 4B, Damini Ma'am wrote a sentence on the board: "Let's play a game to break the ice."
Reena frowned. At home everyone spoke Marathi, and she pictured Ma'am smashing the ice tray from the staff fridge. She raised her hand slowly, then put it down.
Ma'am noticed. "Reena? Something puzzling?"
"Ma'am, which ice?"
A few children giggled. Ma'am did not. "Good question. There is no real ice. It means doing something to make people less shy with each other. What do we do on the first day of term?"
"Say our names and favourite food," Reena said.
"Exactly. That breaks the ice."
Reena wrote it in her notebook, then added a small drawing of a cracked ice cube next to the words "less shy".

qa.q: What did Reena draw in her notebook?
qa.a: A small drawing of a cracked ice cube next to the words "less shy".

qa.q: Why might Reena have raised her hand and then put it down?
qa.a: She was probably confused by the idiom and a little shy or worried about looking silly; she may also have been deciding whether it was worth asking.

qa.q: How did the teacher support Reena, and why did it work?
qa.a: Damini Ma'am noticed the half-raised hand, called the question good, ignored the giggles and linked the idiom to something Reena already knew, which made the meaning stick.

qa.q: What is it like for the children who giggled compared with Reena?
qa.a: For them the idiom may already feel ordinary, so the question seemed funny; for Reena, learning in her second language, the literal picture made real sense.

grounding: A child hears the idiom "break the ice", takes it literally at first, and a teacher explains it using a familiar classroom example.

I was sitting behind Aadhya in science club when Coach Iyer looked out and said, "It's raining cats and dogs, so no football today."
Aadhya shot up and went to the window. She pressed both hands on the glass and stared at the sky for a long time. I couldn't tell if she was looking for the cats or just watching the rain.
When she came back, her mouth was a tight line. She wrote something in her notebook and underlined it twice.
Later at the tap I asked, "What were you looking at?"
She shrugged. "Nothing." Then, "What does it mean? The cats thing?"
I explained it just means very heavy rain. She laughed a bit, but her ears went pink.
The next day I saw "raining cats and dogs = very heavy rain" on her pencil box.
- Omkar

qa.q: Where did Omkar later see the meaning written?
qa.a: On Aadhya's pencil box.

qa.q: What does Aadhya's pink ears and quick "Nothing" suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She may have felt embarrassed that she took the idiom literally, though Omkar cannot be sure; she might also just have wanted to see the heavy rain.

qa.q: What could Coach Iyer try next time when using an idiom?
qa.a: The coach could add a quick plain explanation, like "very heavy rain", so children who are new to the phrase are not left guessing.

qa.q: How does Omkar see Aadhya's reaction, and why can't Omkar be certain?
qa.a: Omkar only sees her go to the window, write something, and turn pink, so Omkar can guess she was puzzled but cannot know her thoughts for sure.

grounding: A classmate observes a child possibly taking "raining cats and dogs" literally, then learning its meaning.

Monday: At the Dharamshala school canteen, Francis patted his stomach. "Mere pet mein chuhe daud rahe hain!" Tenzin, who was still learning Hindi, put down his momo and looked at Francis's stomach with wide eyes. Rats? Running inside? He moved his chair back a little.
Wednesday: Tenzin finally asked. Francis burst out laughing. "No rats! It means I'm very hungry. Like my stomach is so empty, it feels busy." Tenzin laughed too, but still pictured tiny rats with backpacks.
The next Monday: At lunch Tenzin sighed dramatically. "Francis, mere pet mein chuhe daud rahe hain." Francis cheered. Then Tenzin said, "Now you learn one from my Amala," and taught him a Tibetan saying about patience that Francis could not pronounce.

qa.q: What did Francis explain the Hindi saying means?
qa.a: It means he is very hungry.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin move his chair back on Monday?
qa.a: Tenzin was probably alarmed and confused, because he took the idiom literally and pictured rats running inside Francis; he may also have been unsure whether Francis was joking.

qa.q: What helped Tenzin learn the idiom?
qa.a: Asking directly on Wednesday, Francis explaining the picture behind it, and then Tenzin trying it himself the next week.

qa.q: How did the friendship change for Francis by the next Monday?
qa.a: Francis became the learner too, struggling to pronounce Tenzin's Tibetan saying, so the idiom swap went both ways.

grounding: Across three days, a child learning Hindi first takes an idiom literally, then gets it explained, then uses it and shares an idiom from his own culture.

The power went off at nine, just when Joseph had to finish his poem for tomorrow's assembly. The inverter beeped and died.
"Keerthana Chechi, torch!"
His sister held her phone light over his notebook, yawning. "Hurry. Amma will scold if we're still up."
Joseph stared at the dark. The fan had stopped and the whole flat was silent except for a dog somewhere. He wrote: "The night is a thick blanket that swallowed the fan's song."
He crossed it out. Wrote it again.
"Why are you writing about a blanket? It's a poem about our building," Keerthana whispered.
"Because it feels like that," Joseph said. "Heavy and quiet."
She read it twice. "Keep it."
When the light came back, he had four lines, and the last one was: "And I am as still as a lizard on the wall."

qa.q: What did Joseph compare the night to?
qa.a: A thick blanket that swallowed the fan's song.

qa.q: Why did Joseph keep the blanket line even after crossing it out?
qa.a: He wanted a way to express how the dark felt, heavy and quiet; he may also have felt unsure, which is why he crossed it out before writing it again.

qa.q: What helped Joseph finish despite the power cut?
qa.a: His sister held a light, and he used the silence itself as material instead of waiting for the power to return.

qa.q: How did Keerthana's view of the poem change?
qa.a: At first she was puzzled why a building poem had a blanket in it, but after reading it twice she saw the feeling in it and told him to keep it.

grounding: During a power cut, a child uses metaphor and simile to express how the dark felt when direct words fell short.

Gopika sat on the stairs of her building in Kolkata after school, her notebook on her knees. Her friend Disha from the third floor had moved to Pune on Sunday.
When Ma asked what was wrong, Gopika only said, "Nothing." But in her notebook she wrote: "The stairs are as empty as a tiffin box at two o'clock. The moon is a silver coin Disha took with her."
Ma sat down next to her and read over her shoulder. "Disha took the moon?"
"She used to count coins with me on these stairs," Gopika said, and her chin wobbled.
Ma put her arm round her. They read the lines together twice.
That night Gopika copied the poem neatly and asked Ma to send a photo of it to Disha's mother.

qa.q: What did Gopika say the moon was in her notebook?
qa.a: A silver coin Disha took with her.

qa.q: What does Gopika's wobbling chin suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She was probably sad and missing Disha, a feeling she could not say out loud but could put into her metaphors.

qa.q: How did Ma support Gopika, and why did it help?
qa.a: Ma sat beside her and asked about the line instead of pushing for an answer, which let Gopika explain her feelings through the poem.

qa.q: What might it mean for Disha to receive the poem?
qa.a: Disha might feel missed and loved, knowing Gopika still thinks of their coin counting on the stairs.

grounding: A child uses similes and metaphors to express missing a friend she could not describe directly.

"Joseph, it's the bhajan from the temple on Friday. I can't get it out of my head."
"What does it do? You were smiling with your eyes shut."
"When everyone claps together and Amma sings the high part, my stomach goes quiet. Like after a big drink of water."

"That's like our last aarti."
"Sing me the clapping part?"
"Only if you sing me the fast one."
They sang, badly, in the corridor, till the bell rang.

qa.a: A teacher could give time for children to share what their songs feel like, without saying one feeling is the right one.

qa.a: Joseph's loud hymn makes him feel excited, while Gopika's bhajan calms her, showing that shared singing can bring different feelings to each child.

I remember the Ganpati aarti in our building courtyard when I was in Class 3. Everyone stood in a circle with little brass lamps, and Kaka banged the drum.
I didn't know all the words. So I just clapped and sang the "Jai Dev" part really loudly. My arms had goosebumps. I felt like I was part of something much bigger than me.
Tanuja, from the flat opposite, stood beside me. She kept giggling and nudging me. At first I thought she was making fun. Later she told me she loved the drum so much she wanted to dance, but everyone was standing still.
We both came every evening that week. Tanuja for the drum, me for the singing.
- Shankar

qa.a: Shankar first worried she was making fun, but she was actually excited because she loved the drum and wanted to dance.

qa.q: How did Tanuja experience the aarti differently from Shankar?
qa.a: Tanuja was drawn to the drum and felt like dancing, while Shankar felt goosebumps from singing with everyone.

Assembly note, Friday
This morning Class 5 led the carol for the school's winter assembly.
Varun sang with his eyes closed and swayed a little. After the last line he whispered, "It feels like being hugged."
Tarun stood stiff at the end of the row and mostly mouthed the words. I wondered if he was uncomfortable or unwell.
Afterward I asked him quietly. He said he liked the part where everyone clapped at the end, but his own voice felt too loud in his ears.
Next week I will let children choose to sing, hum, or keep the beat on the tambourine. Tarun already asked for the tambourine.
- Ms Pereira, music teacher

qa.a: She planned to let children sing, hum or keep the beat, because it allows each child to join the group in the way that feels right.

qa.q: How did Varun experience the carol compared with Tarun?
qa.a: Varun felt comforted and joyful, like being hugged, while Tarun was uneasy with his voice but still enjoyed the shared clapping.

passage: "When my Thatha died, Seema, I was about your age. For thirteen days our house was full: relatives sleeping on mats, the lamp always burning, Amma's cousins singing low songs at dusk. I didn't understand why nobody cooked anything sweet. I asked Amma, 'Where did Thatha go?' She didn't say he was sleeping. She said, 'His body stopped working, Vasudha. It had rained all morning, and Nani's small house in the town was packed for the prayer meeting. Wet chappals piled at the door; the fan couldn't cope.
Bhavna squeezed between aunties on the floor. Everyone was silent while the pandit read from a book, and Nani sat very still in a white saree.
Bhavna whispered to her Mama Ujjwal, "Will Nana come back if we pray?"
Ujjwal took a breath. "No, beta. Nana's body stopped working. He won't come back. We pray to remember him and to help us feel less alone."
Bhavna nodded, eyes wet. Twenty minutes later she was under the stairs with her cousin, giggling over a lizard. Then she saw Nana's walking stick by the door and went quiet again.

qa.q: Where was Bhavna when she was giggling with her cousin?
qa.a: Under the stairs.

qa.q: How can you tell Bhavna feels sad in bursts rather than all the time?
qa.a: Her eyes are wet after Ujjwal's answer, then she giggles over a lizard, then goes quiet again at the sight of Nana's walking stick, showing sadness that comes and goes.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do that helped Bhavna understand?
qa.a: He gave a simple, honest answer that Nana would not come back and explained the prayer is for remembering, instead of confusing her.

qa.q: What is it like for Nani during the prayer meeting?
qa.a: Nani sits very still in white, likely deep in grief, while the crowded house and noise go on around her.

grounding: A child at a crowded prayer meeting asks what death means, gets an honest answer, and grieves in short bursts between play.

On the first day of term at the Deaf school in Bristol, a new girl stood by the classroom door, holding her bag straps tight. Chidi walked up, signed a question, and pointed at her.
She fingerspelled slowly: F-R-E-Y-A.
Chidi copied it letter by letter, grinning. Then he spelled his own name back, fast, the way he had done a hundred times.
At break the class argued about what Freya's name sign should be. Someone suggested a sign near the head, because of her springy curls. Freya laughed and shook her curls. Chidi nodded hard.
In science, Mr Owens fingerspelled a new word, V-O-L-C-A-N-O. The class had no shared sign for it yet, so everybody spelled it out until Chidi made up one with a bursting hand. Freya used it straight away.

qa.q: What new word did Mr Owens fingerspell in science?
qa.a: V-O-L-C-A-N-O, the word volcano.

qa.q: How can you tell Freya's mood changed during the day?
qa.a: She held her bag straps tight at the door, which suggests she felt nervous, but at break she laughed and shook her curls, which suggests she felt pleased and included. She may also simply have found the argument funny.

qa.q: What did the class do when a word had no shared sign yet?
qa.a: They fingerspelled it until Chidi made up a sign, which shows fingerspelling filling a gap inside a full language rather than replacing it.

qa.a: Everyone would have to spell her name letter by letter each time, which is slower and might leave her feeling less like part of the group.

grounding: The Deaf classroom shows children fingerspelling a new name and a new word, and the community giving the newcomer a name sign.

At my cousin's wedding in Lucknow, I kept watching Zeenat Baji and her Deaf friends at the corner table.
When the groom walked in, Zeenat spelled something with her fingers, very quickly, and pointed at the stage. Her friends nodded, and one of them made a small sign near the chin. After that nobody spelled it again. They used that sign every time they talked about him.
I don't know sign language, so I couldn't tell what they were saying. But Zeenat's hands were fast and her eyebrows kept jumping up, like she was telling a good story.

qa.q: What did one of Zeenat's friends do after she fingerspelled?
qa.a: One of them made a small sign near the chin.

qa.q: What does Zeenat's signing suggest about her mood, and why can't Hafsa be sure?
qa.a: Her fast hands and jumping eyebrows suggest she felt excited and amused, maybe sharing a joke about the groom, but Hafsa does not know sign language and can only guess from what is visible.

qa.q: What could Hafsa try at the next family gathering?
qa.a: Hafsa could ask Zeenat to teach a few more signs, including the chin sign, instead of guessing what the group meant.

qa.q: How do Zeenat's friends seem to treat the new chin sign?
qa.a: They seem to accept it at once as their shared name for the groom, using it every time instead of spelling his name again.

grounding: An observer sees a signer fingerspell a name once before her friends settle on a name sign within their own language.

Jana had just moved in next door to Siddiq's family in Berlin. The first time Siddiq signed to her, Jana looked down at the floor, trying to be polite. Siddiq stopped and waved his hand gently in front of her face.
She looked up. He signed again, slower, and this time she watched his hands, then his face. She didn't understand much, but he smiled.
The next day, Jana saw Siddiq's mother tap his shoulder to get his attention. At dinner his little brother flicked the kitchen lights, and everyone turned to him at once.
"I thought staring was rude," Jana told her own mother later. "But for them, looking is listening."
The next time Siddiq signed, Jana kept her eyes on his hands and face the whole way through.

qa.q: How did Siddiq's little brother get everyone's attention at dinner?
qa.a: He flicked the kitchen lights, and everyone turned to him at once.

qa.q: Why did Jana look down at the floor at first?
qa.a: She wanted to be polite and was probably shy and unsure, because where she came from staring felt rude; she did not yet know that for a signer, looking away can seem like not listening.

qa.q: What helped Jana change how she paid attention?
qa.a: Watching how Siddiq's family tapped shoulders, flicked lights and all turned to look showed her that watching the signer is the respectful way to listen.

qa.q: How might Siddiq have felt when Jana first looked at the floor?
qa.a: He might have felt ignored or puzzled, since in his family looking at hands and face is how people listen.

grounding: A child learns that signers get attention by waving, tapping or flicking lights, and that keeping eyes on the signer is respectful.

In the mixed class at the Pune school, Mrs Kale asked everyone to answer in turn. Tanuja, who is Deaf, had her hand up, but the hearing children kept talking over each other.
She reached over and flicked the classroom light switch twice. Everyone turned, startled.
Yash frowned. "Why did she do that?" he whispered.
The interpreter signed to Tanuja and answered him quietly: "That's how signers get a group's attention. Like calling out, but for eyes."
Tanuja began signing her answer. Yash kept staring at the interpreter, then noticed Tanuja glancing at his face, checking. He moved his eyes to her hands and face instead.
At the end, Tanuja caught his eye and smiled. Yash signed "thank you" clumsily. She laughed and showed him the right way.

qa.q: How many times did Tanuja flick the light switch?
qa.a: She flicked it twice.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when the lights flicked?
qa.a: Yash felt startled and confused, and perhaps a little annoyed, because he did not yet know flicking lights is a normal way for a signer to get attention.

qa.q: How could a teacher help the hearing children take turns fairly with Tanuja?
qa.a: Mrs Kale could explain the light flick and waving beforehand, stop talk-overs, and remind everyone to watch the signer's hands and face during her turn.

qa.q: If you were Tanuja, what would you want from the class?
qa.a: You would want people to notice your raised hand without needing the lights, and to look at you rather than only at the interpreter while you answer.

grounding: A classroom shows a Deaf child getting attention by flicking lights, and a hearing classmate learning to keep his gaze on the signer.

qa.a: Chacha seems amused rather than hurt, since everyone laughed and he playfully threw a napkin at Amandeep.

grounding: An observer at a family lunch learns that a signer waves or taps for attention and that watching hands and face is respectful.

In Oslo, Jin sat at the kitchen table chewing her pencil. At school she had shouted at her friend Astrid for snapping her favourite blue crayon, and Astrid had walked away without a word. Now Jin's stomach felt knotted, but every time she practised saying sorry out loud, her throat closed up.
So she took a pink card and wrote: "Sorry I yelled. It was only a crayon. I miss drawing with you. Friends again?"
She drew a tiny broken crayon with a plaster on it.
The next morning she slipped the card into Astrid's pencil case and hurried to her seat.
At lunch Astrid found it, read it twice, and wrote underneath: "Friends! I'll bring my crayons tomorrow 🙂"
Jin read the reply under the desk and grinned all afternoon.

qa.q: What did Jin draw on the card?
qa.a: A tiny broken crayon with a plaster on it.

qa.q: Why did Jin write the apology instead of saying it?
qa.a: Jin felt guilty and embarrassed, and every time she tried to say sorry aloud her throat closed up, so writing was easier than speaking.

qa.q: What made Jin's note work well?
qa.a: It was short and honest: it owned the yelling, said the crayon mattered less than the friendship, and asked a simple question Astrid could answer.

qa.q: How might Astrid have felt walking away and then finding the card?
qa.a: Astrid was probably hurt when she walked away, and the card likely made her feel relieved and cared for, so replying in writing felt easy.

grounding: A child writes a note to say sorry because the feeling is hard to say aloud, and her friend replies in writing.

Every night at the girls' hostel, Rashmi wrote in her green diary: about missing Amma's rasam, her little brother's silly jokes, and the heavy feeling after lights out.
One evening she left it open on her bed and went to brush her teeth.
Her roommate Charu came in, saw the open page, and stopped. Her eyes caught the first line. Then she closed the diary and put it back on the pillow.
When Rashmi returned, Charu said, "Your diary was open. I shut it. I read one line by mistake, sorry."
Rashmi's face went red. "Which line?"

Rashmi let out a breath. "Thanks. It's... private."
"I keep one too," Charu said. "Under my mattress."
After that they talked about home sometimes, but never about each other's diaries.

qa.q: Where does Charu keep her own diary?
qa.a: Under her mattress.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she asked "Which line?"
qa.a: Rashmi felt embarrassed and anxious that her private feelings about home had been read, and then relieved when Charu said it was only "Dear diary".

qa.q: What did Charu do well?
qa.a: She shut the diary instead of reading on, and told Rashmi honestly, which respected Rashmi's privacy and kept her trust.

qa.q: How might the friendship have changed if Charu had read the whole diary?
qa.a: Rashmi might have felt exposed and stopped writing freely, and she might not have trusted Charu enough to talk about home later.

grounding: A hostel child uses a diary for feelings that are hard to say aloud, and a roommate respects its privacy.
